EXCLUSIVE: Christianity Today faces $3 million deficit as financial troubles threaten magazine’s future

By Daniel Silliman
  • November 12, 2026
  • 7:02 pm CST
  • 7 Comments
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:45
Instaread

Disclosure: Reporter Daniel Silliman worked as Christianity Today’s news editor from 2019 to 2025. He quit after six years, citing practical and philosophical disagreements. None of those disagreements were directly related to the financial decisions reported here.

Christianity Today (CT), frequently described as the flagship of American evangelicalism, is teetering on the brink of a financial crisis.

The 70-year-old magazine expects to end 2026 with a $3 million deficit, according to an internal financial report obtained by Roys Report (RR). A second report shows revenue from subscriptions, advertising and product sales is running $80,000 to $90,000 below monthly benchmarks.

Ambitious plans to grow revenue 15% annually have floundered. CT’s new smartphone app, for example, cost more than $200,000 to develop but has brought in only about 100 new subscriptions, according to current and former staff with detailed knowledge of internal discussions.

President Nicole Martin and Chief Operating Officer Tom Addington told staff this summer that they would have to reduce CT’s annual spending from $18 million, when Martin became president in 2025, to $14 million next year.

However, the “balanced budget” proposed for 2027 depends on increases of nearly $1 million in donations and $1 million in other revenue.

The publication’s circulation numbers have not risen in more than a decade, and the senior vice president of marketing was laid off last month. The person responsible for selling two-thirds of CT’s ads was also laid off, along with about a dozen other staff members. CT’s director of advertising quit last week.

Other staff are heading for the exits. Theologian Russell Moore — whose podcast “The Russell Moore Show” has been one of the few to make money and whose articles are among the most read — has informed CT he is leaving after Thanksgiving.

CT has relied in recent years on about 500 major donors and about a dozen grants for financial sustainability, internal records show. Donors appear hesitant to give more money on top of the $26.5 million pledged in the last three years, according to current and former staff. New fundraising efforts, including a “Billy Graham legacy fund,” have been announced, then abandoned due to a lack of interest.

“They’re spiraling,” one former vice president told RR, “and grasping at straws to stay afloat.”

Martin told RR this week that CT has been through some hard times and has had to make some admittedly tough decisions. But she believes the organization is now stronger than it has been in years and is looking forward to a bright future.

“The painful yet necessary work of reductions has stabilized our budget,” Martin said in an email. “CT’s mission has not changed in 70 years, and we are now positioned financially and operationally to continue that legacy into the future.”

An economic story

Critics of CT have long predicted its demise. When evangelist Billy Graham launched the magazine in 1956 — as part of a larger project to bring together evangelicals from different denominations — conservatives said it should really be called “Christianity Astray.” Liberal detractors dubbed it “Christianity Yesterday.” Both sides prophesied it would be a failure.

CT staff at every level have wondered in recent years if those pessimistic predictions are finally coming true. Perhaps the magazine is too far to the left or too far to the right. Perhaps it is too political or not political enough to survive this specific moment in history.

Maybe not enough people are interested in this brand of Christianity.

But when they are pressed to explain what is happening, people who poured their hearts and souls into CT tell an economic story.

RR interviewed two dozen current and former staff members who have worked at every level. Many were granted anonymity to talk freely about private discussions and decisions without endangering their current jobs or future employment. Every detail reported here has been confirmed by two or more sources with direct knowledge of the information.

RR also reviewed internal financial reports, fundraising reports, tax records, project proposals, detailed notes of meetings and automated updates on readership, subscriptions and revenue.

The documents and testimonies tell a story of a legacy media organization struggling through industry-wide economic turmoil. CT executives have made some bold decisions, some bad decisions and some stupid mistakes as they navigated market headwinds, current and former staff say.

They mourn what looks like an oncoming catastrophe.

“My last day was Friday, and I spent Saturday and Sunday crying,” Caitlin Edwards, former director of marketing and advertising, told RR. “I realized how much grief I’ve been holding — grief and sadness. I want CT to survive and thrive. At this point, I don’t see how that happens.”

Turn to donations

The financial story starts with the subprime mortgage crisis in 2008. When the housing bubble burst, the impact hit media companies — already struggling to adapt to challenges posed by the internet — especially hard. More than 140 newspapers and 360 magazines ceased publishing in 2009.

CT lost one-third of its advertising revenue and one-quarter of its subscriptions, tax records show. The magazine laid off 42 of the 162 people who worked there. The crisis might have been worse, but then-President Harold Smith solicited several hundred thousand dollars in donations.

Then he kept raising money.

At first, donations covered 2% of the budget. Then 5%. Then closer to 15%, according to tax records.

When Timothy Dalrymple replaced Smith as CT president in 2019, advertising brought in $3.2 million, subscriptions $2.4 million and the sale of Sunday school curriculum and tax manuals earned another $2.4 million. A bit more than 14% of the budget — about $1.3 million — came from “contributions and grants.”

Dalrymple had ideas about growing that fourth stream of revenue. A Stanford University graduate with a doctorate in the philosophy of religion from Harvard University, he was vice president of business development at Patheos when the blogging startup grew through fundraising.

At CT, Dalrymple more than doubled contributions and grants revenue in two years. In 2021, tax records show $2.7 million in new philanthropic investments.

By 2023, after Dalrymple had been at the helm for four years, CT’s total revenue had grown from $9.7 million to $18.3 million. Almost all that increase came from donations.

“It’s entirely appropriate for a nonprofit to have healthy philanthropic collections,” Dalrymple wrote in a board report obtained by RR. “In a market landscape where numerous media organizations have closed or downsized significantly, we are grateful to God that our story has been different.”

But advertising revenue declined 12.5% in that same time period. Subscription revenue was up, thanks to a rate hike from $39 to $59, but paid circulation was dropping. CT lost a total of about 5,500 subscribers during COVID-19, another 3,500 from 2021 to 2022, and a few thousand more by the end of the following year.

Contributions and grants made up more than 50% of CT’s total 2023 revenue.

“Cool new stuff”

Critics of CT — notably Daily Wire reporter Megan Basham, who wrote the book “Shepherds for Sale” — have accused the magazine of betraying evangelicalism and embracing “a leftist agenda” to get grant money.

Inside CT, current and former staff say they never felt the mission changed. What they saw was a massive influx of funds going to “cool new stuff.” CT now had its own version of a tech incubator.

What if CT had a literary magazine that appealed to young people? What if it had editors around the world who could seek out the “sages and storytellers” of the global church? Could CT have its own version of Netflix? Or National Geographic?

“The Global Issue,” CT’s version of National Geographic, received an initial budget of $1.2 million, funded by grants. Dalrymple dreamed the annual publication would become a “signature product” and deemed it “critical to our strategic plan going forward.”

The special publication, released in 2022 and 2024, did not have any advertising. It lacked a major marketing push to promote the new product to non-subscribers and grow the CT audience. There was, however, a donor drive.

One employee described the economic model as “balancing a chair on one leg forever.”

Some of the new grant-and-donor-funded projects did include plans to increase revenue. Even then, the sustainability part of the plan never got executed.

CT used grants, for example, to launch a project to translate articles into Spanish, Portuguese, Chinese, Indonesian, Korean and other languages. CT Global Editorial Director Jeremy Weber argued the project would prove people around the world were hungry for CT content. The “Global Initiative” then added editors dedicated to East Asia, Southeast Asia, South Asia and China.

Their work found readers. But they rarely became subscribers.

“We got to a point where one-third of all readers were outside the United States,” former CT Global Managing Editor Morgan Lee told RR. “We struggled to get the digital infrastructure that would create a pathway to monetize those readers. We couldn’t get it prioritized. It was a big bummer.”

Today, Singapore is the only country in Asia with more than 200 CT subscribers. Lee was laid off last year. The international editor who succeeded her quit this month. CT is not currently advertising that job opening, nor any job openings.

Hit podcast did not make money

Some of the “cool new stuff” did find a large audience. “The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill” podcast, for example, was a massive hit. CT reported more than 2.5 million downloads of the first seven episodes in 2021, making the series the third most popular podcast in the country.

But “The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill” did not make money.

CT’s media department blamed the people in advertising: They did not know how to sell podcast ads, nor did they seem especially invested in the new advertising opportunity.

CT’s advertising department blamed the podcasters: When the show proved to be popular, unannounced delays in the release of new episodes forced CT to offer refunds to advertisers. At least one major company backed out, reportedly because of poor planning and poor communication.

There was no substantive plan to turn the podcast listeners into CT subscribers, either. When host Mike Cosper said at the end of some episodes, “Subscriptions to CT are one of the best ways to support this kind of journalism,” few listeners took the hint.

The popularity of “The Rise and Fall of Mars Hill” had no apparent impact on the steady decline of paid subscriptions, as shown by tax records.

Other podcasts had an even more difficult time securing advertising dollars and relied heavily on grant and donor funding. Some struggled to find listeners. One series, “This Great & Complicated Place,” ended up costing about $250 per download.

According to an internal audit, podcast revenue declined from an average of about $40,000 per month in early 2022 to less than $20,000 in 2024. Costs during that same period increased from $10,000 per month to about $37,000.

Expenses kept going up

Each new project and initiative came with additional hires, who were funded, at least at first, by grants. People brought on to work on these projects told RR their contracts were not tied to the temporary funding, so they assumed that when the grants ended, they would continue working at CT.

The number of supervisors also increased during this time. In 2019, eight people at CT earned more than $100,000 per year. In 2024, the most recent year for which tax records are available, CT reported paying six-figure salaries to 14 people.

Operations, meanwhile, were strained to the point of breaking, according to current and former staff. Some of those breaks had significant financial consequences.

A switch to new billing software messed up advertising revenue for months. A change in subscription management systems resulted in the loss of some credit card data, disrupting automated renewals. That led to a loss of more than 500 subscriptions every month for two years — reducing the total number of paid subscribers from 66,000 to about 43,000. A change in accounting software meant that historic trend data went missing from the reports the finance department was giving to executives.

At the same time, finances became more complicated. Grants and many donations could only be spent on specific purposes, but those restrictions were regularly renegotiated. Some funds, including a pandemic-era employee-retention tax credit, were recorded in CT’s ledgers before they were received. Pledged money did not always come in on schedule, creating unexpected pinches in cash flow.

An outside firm, looking at CT’s financial situation in March 2025, noted the bulk of its revenue was “complex and highly variable.” The report also found that accurate information about CT finances seemed “hard to pin down.”

Also in early 2025, Dalrymple noted what he called “elevated rates of spending,” according to former staff who worked with him. He and Martin, who would replace him as president the following year, went through credit card statements and bank records line by line and discovered about $850,000 of “missing expenses.”

Eight people were laid off later that month.

Dalrymple warned the board in April that CT should prepare for a notable drop in philanthropic revenue after a successful fundraising campaign brought in $32 million.

“We … need rising non-philanthropic revenue to counterbalance diminishing philanthropic revenue,” Dalrymple wrote. “Our goal is to grow non-philanthropic revenue at a compounding rate of 15%.”

Dalrymple expressed confidence that this optimistic goal — outpacing the growth of some of the country’s leading media organizations, including The Atlantic and The New York Times — was achievable.

He said the newly hired vice president of marketing and a subscription-rate hike from $59 to $72 would lead to the “healthy growth” of that revenue stream. Advertising would increase with “exciting new podcasts.” And the relaunch of two publications, CT Pastors and Leadership Journal, promised to “both serve the church and improve our resources revenue.”

The fourth stream of revenue, philanthropy, could probably be counted on for about $5 million per year, Dalrymple said.

He left CT in June 2025 to head up the John Templeton Foundation. He told RR this week he thinks his analysis of CT’s financial future was fundamentally correct. But he also has a greater appreciation, in retrospect, for the financial challenges CT was facing.

“The fact that CT has not only endured but grown through the last decade of market turbulence, when so many other media organizations have expired or diminished, is eloquent testimony to the generosity of its supporters and the skill of its team,” Dalrymple said in an email. “CT remains a vital institution, and, speaking personally, I look forward to seeing its future under current leadership.”

Current leadership cuts more

In August 2025, interim president Tom Addington announced in a staff meeting that an outside accounting firm had just discovered more “missing expenses.” He said CT would need to make more cuts and major changes, adjusting its editorial vision and rethinking the funding model that relied so much on philanthropy.

Fourteen more people were laid off in September, including several who oversaw the projects Dalrymple had said could lead to 15% annual growth.

“It was a dire, dire year,” a former editor told RR. “You hope somebody has a plan. Maybe there’s a secret plan? There is no plan.”

Addington, who became chief operating officer when Martin was named president, blamed the crisis on complex finances and hidden, elevated rates of spending.

But even after every department made budget cuts, Addington told staff that it was difficult to get a full picture of the financial situation. CT laid off about a dozen more people ahead of its 70th anniversary, celebrated by the remaining staff in Washington, D.C., in September 2026.

“I would say, with lament, that we see through a glass darkly,” Addington said, according to detailed notes from a meeting.

An internal audit warns of a looming “zero day” that could come as soon as next year, according to staff who saw the report or heard it discussed. The only good news on the financial horizon is a $4 million payment from the faith-based tech company Gloo, due in March 2027.

Staff say they were told that CT must work to wean itself off contributions and grants, and go back to the older revenue model, with most funds coming from subscriptions, advertising and product sales.

Current employees told RR that CT has increased the number of ads on the website. Other than that, it is not clear where new revenue is supposed to come from. Nor is it clear there will be enough people left at CT to execute a plan, if executives have one.

The 2027 budget also calls for fundraising to continue providing 50% of CT’s operating expenses.

According to Addington, the adjustment of the economic model will take about three years. People who have worked on CT’s funding say they are not sure the organization can last that long.

“Addressing the organization’s immediate financial challenges will require bold, strategic fundraising efforts,” Amy Richardson, former CT director of donor engagement, told RR. “I have the greatest respect for Nicole Martin and believe she is an exceptional leader with a deep commitment to the mission of Christianity Today. That said, in my opinion, there is a significant gap between the fundraising approach the organization feels prepared to pursue and the level of investment, staffing and bold strategy that will be required.”

Addington and Martin will present the 2027 budget to the board next week.

Daniel Silliman is senior reporter/editor at Roys Report. He began his two decades in journalism covering crime in Atlanta and has since led major investigations into abuse and misconduct in Christian contexts. Daniel and his wife live in Johnson City, Tennessee.
